atlas_note: ATLAS techniques describe attacks on AI systems; evading a bot check with automation has no ATLAS counterpart.
detection_notes: MITRE's analytic for this technique says CAPTCHA telemetry alone cannot separate a person from a solver, so look at what the session does after the check. Useful signals are sign-up or login bursts that share an IP range, ASN, residential proxy pool or browser fingerprint; accounts that pass the check and then move straight to the abuse the check protects (bulk messages, trial resource creation, form spam); and challenge pass rates or solve times that shift sharply for one form or one client population. Bot-management and WAF logs, account-creation logs and the protected application's own audit log are the sources to join.
name: Anti-Automation Evasion
narrative: Anyone who runs a sign-up form, a login page or a ticket queue has met this problem: the CAPTCHA or bot check meant to keep scripts out is now something an attacker can buy as a service or hand to an AI browser agent. This technique covers getting automated traffic past those checks, either by completing the challenge with a solver (T1696.001) or by behaving enough like a person that no challenge is shown (T1696.002).

The practical lesson for defenders is that a passed check is weak evidence that a person is present. Bot checks still raise the cost of abuse, but they work best as one signal among several rather than as the gate itself.

atlas_note: No ATLAS counterpart: the solver is a tool used against a web control, not an attack on an AI system.
detection_notes: A solved challenge looks the same whether a person, a script or a paid solving service answered it, which is why MITRE's analytic stops at the provider's own bot score. Watch the steps around the challenge instead: challenge tokens redeemed from a different IP or client than the one that requested them, solve times that are unusually uniform, many new accounts with the same payment, email-domain or naming pattern, and trial or free-tier resources that start heavy compute (for example cryptocurrency mining) soon after sign-up.
name: Automate CAPTCHA Completion
narrative: Solving a CAPTCHA no longer takes a person at the keyboard. Solver services, browser-automation frameworks and image or audio recognition models return a valid answer in seconds, so one operator can create accounts or submit forms at the scale the challenge was meant to stop.

Unit 42's 2023 report on PurpleUrchin, run by the group it calls Automated Libra, describes a freejacking operation that bypassed CAPTCHA while signing up for limited-time cloud trials to mine cryptocurrency.

atlas_note: No ATLAS counterpart: mimicking a human visitor targets a web control, not an AI system.
detection_notes: MITRE publishes an analytic that notes there is no target-side behavioral detection based only on CAPTCHA telemetry, so detection has to come from the rest of the session. Look for sessions that are never challenged yet show automation traits (headless or instrumented browser markers, fingerprints that repeat across many addresses, identical navigation paths), contact-form or chat-widget submissions that arrive in volume with generated text, and traffic from residential proxy ranges that does not match the site's normal audience.
name: Avoid CAPTCHA
narrative: Many bot defenses only show a challenge when a session already looks suspicious. Avoiding the CAPTCHA means never reaching that threshold: replaying real browser fingerprints, pacing requests, moving the pointer and typing with human timing, and rotating through residential addresses.

SentinelLabs' 2025 AkiraBot report describes a spam framework that targeted hCAPTCHA and reCAPTCHA and carried browser fingerprints so its traffic would look like a legitimate visitor's. SentinelLabs assessed that it targeted more than 400,000 websites.

atlas_note: No ATLAS counterpart: the target is an account credential, not an AI system.
detection_notes: MITRE ships analytics for identity-provider, Office Suite and SaaS logs. In practice, alert on every app-specific password creation for accounts that have no approved need for one, and correlate it with sign-ins through legacy or non-MFA protocols (IMAP, POP, SMTP AUTH and similar) from a new source within a short window. Where the provider allows it, turn app-specific passwords off for most users and review the ones that remain; a request from "IT" or an outside contact to create one and share it is a phishing signal on its own.
name: Steal Application Specific Passwords
narrative: Application-specific passwords exist so that an old mail client or device that cannot do multifactor prompts can still sign in. That makes them a quiet way around MFA: a password the user creates once, that the provider accepts without a second factor, and that keeps working until someone revokes it.

Citizen Lab and Google reported in June 2025 that an attacker posing as a U.S. State Department employee persuaded a researcher to create app-specific passwords and send them over, and Google attributed the activity to a Russian state-backed operator. ATT&CK lists APT42 as a procedure example.

atlas_note: The same behavior seen from the AI system's side: prompt injection delivered through retrieved content, and poisoning of the context an agent works from.
detection_notes: Keep a log that ties each agent action to the content it had just retrieved: the prompt, the retrieved documents or URLs, and every tool call with its arguments. Alert when a tool call (sending mail, changing code, calling an external URL) follows retrieval of outside content and was not part of the user's request; scan inbound email, tickets, issues and shared documents for instruction-like text aimed at a model, including hidden or zero-width text; and treat unexpected agent writes to repositories or CI settings as an incident until shown otherwise.
name: Indirect Prompt Injection
narrative: When a copilot or agent reads a web page, an email, a ticket or a pull request on someone's behalf, whoever wrote that content gets a say in what the model does next. Indirect prompt injection hides instructions in that content, often in text a person will not notice (HTML comments, white-on-white text, alt text, metadata), and waits for an AI system to retrieve it.

Unit 42 reported web-based indirect prompt injection aimed at AI agents in the wild in March 2026, and Snyk's "Clinejection" write-up describes an AI bot in a GitHub Actions workflow being steered into a supply-chain attack. The attacker never touches the model directly; the agent's own reading does the delivery.

atlas_note: ATLAS's view of the same act: a prompt injected straight into the model, and jailbreaking it past its safety controls.
detection_notes: For assistants your organization runs, log prompts and responses at an AI gateway and review accounts that show repeated refusals followed by success, override phrasing ("ignore", "developer mode", "system prompt"), attempts to read the system prompt, or claims of authorization (pentest, red team) without a matching record. For agents with tools, the higher-value signal is what the model does after the prompt: tool calls, code execution or data access that the user's role would not normally produce.
name: Direct Prompt Injection
narrative: Direct prompt injection is the attacker typing into the model themselves: role-play framings, "ignore your previous instructions", requests split into harmless-looking pieces, or claims to be a security tester, all aimed at getting the model to do what its safeguards or its operator would refuse.

ATT&CK lists two campaigns as procedure examples: the espionage campaign Anthropic described in November 2025 as the first reported AI-orchestrated one, and an AI-assisted breach of Mexican government infrastructure described in an April 2026 report. In both, prompting a model past its safeguards was part of how the operators worked.

atlas_note: ATLAS's exfiltration techniques for the same path: data sent out through an agent's tool calls, or through the AI user interface itself.
detection_notes: MITRE ships three analytics that follow data from the agent's access to a transfer outside approved flows. To make them workable, keep an inventory of each agent's tools, data scopes and allowed destinations; log tool calls with arguments; and alert on agent-initiated transfers to new domains, URLs with long encoded query strings, and outbound messages or uploads that quote content the agent retrieved from a sensitive store. Restricting what an agent may render or fetch (no arbitrary image or link URLs) closes the quietest channel.
name: AI-Enabled Exfiltration
narrative: An enterprise agent that can read mail, search a document store and call tools already holds everything an exfiltration path needs. This technique covers turning that agent against its owner, usually through a direct or indirect prompt injection, so that it sends data out through a tool it is allowed to use: an email, a web request, a rendered image or link whose URL carries the data, or a write to an outside repository.

The arXiv paper "The Framing Gap" (August 2026) shows indirect prompt-injection exfiltration getting past surface-level defenses in tool-using agents, Google's April 2026 survey describes the prompt injections already planted on public web pages, and Barracuda reported email attacks in October 2026 written to reach both the human reader and an AI assistant in the same message.

atlas_note: The retrieval side of the same idea: content crafted to be retrieved by an AI system, and poisoning of a retrieval-augmented generation corpus.
detection_notes: MITRE's analytic states that the target cannot reliably tell this staging apart from ordinary publishing using its own telemetry. What an organization can watch: AI answers and AI search results that mention its brand, support numbers or download locations (checked on a schedule, the way brand-protection teams already watch search ads); newly registered or lookalike domains that start appearing in those answers; and, on endpoints, users who paste a command into a shell or Run dialog shortly after visiting an AI assistant or answer page.
name: AI Result Poisoning
narrative: Search poisoning has a new target: the answer box. Adversaries publish pages, forum posts and listings written so that AI search features and chat assistants pick them up and repeat them, putting a phishing site, a fake support number or a malicious download into an answer the user already trusts.

Netcraft reported in August 2026 that threat actors were finding their way into AI summaries, and Lasso Security showed how generative engine optimization (GEO) can push harmful claims into AI-generated answers. Because the staging happens on the open web before any victim system is involved, ATT&CK files it under Resource Development.

atlas_note: ATLAS describes the defender's model as the victim: evading an AI model, here by prompt injection carried in the sample it reads.
detection_notes: Scan samples, logs and tickets for natural-language text addressed to a model (role markers, "system:" blocks, instructions to ignore or classify as benign) and treat its presence as a strong malicious indicator in itself. Compare LLM triage verdicts with static, sandbox and reputation results and send disagreements to a person; alert when an automated triage run aborts, times out or returns an empty result on a sample; and protect the configuration of autonomous defensive tooling the way you protect EDR policy.
name: Impair Autonomous Defenses
narrative: Security teams now hand first-pass triage of samples, alerts and logs to LLM-based assistants. Malware authors have noticed: this technique is planting text aimed at that assistant, such as fake system messages or notes claiming the file is a benign test, so that the automated analyst skips the sample, misreads it or stops early.

SentinelLabs reported in June 2026 on macOS.Gaslight, a DPRK-linked Rust backdoor that embeds 38 fabricated system messages spoofing an LLM triage harness while hiding a credential stealer and Telegram command and control. The target is the defender's automation, not the sandbox.
